cases.learnTitle: Only mild irregularity of the left coronary system (expert box, under 50%)
cases.contextSource: Dataset description (one hospital's catheterisation laboratory); individual histories are in the dataset's spreadsheet and are not used here.
cases.referenceSummary: The dataset's cardiologists boxed only milder lesions (under 50%) on this frame; there is no narrowing of 50% or more to find here. The boxes are rectangles around a lesion, not outlines. Single hospital, 42 patients; a single frame of a run filmed at 10 frames per second. The projection angle is not distributed.
cases.learnNotes: Two arteries arise from the aortic root. The right coronary artery is usually a single long vessel that runs down the right side of the heart and curves under it to the back wall. The left main artery is a short trunk that divides into the left anterior descending artery (down the front of the heart towards the apex, with diagonal branches) and the left circumflex artery (round the left side, with obtuse marginal branches); sometimes a third, intermediate branch arises between them. A coronary stenosis is a narrowing of the lumen of an artery, most often from atherosclerotic plaque in the wall. An invasive angiogram shows only the lumen, filled with contrast, so a stenosis appears where the dark column of contrast becomes narrower than the normal vessel next to it: a short pinch, a long tapering, or an irregular edge. Its degree is the percentage loss of diameter against that normal reference; a narrowing of 70% or more is generally treated as obstructive and one of 50 to 69% as intermediate, where the picture alone predicts poorly whether blood flow is limited. Whether a narrowing limits flow also depends on its length, its place and the territory it supplies, which a single frame cannot tell you. A 99% narrowing leaves a hair-thin channel; in a total occlusion the vessel stops and may be filled further on from other arteries. Pitfalls: a vessel seen end-on or overlapped by another vessel hides or imitates a narrowing, so every artery is looked at in several projections; the catheter tip, the spine and the diaphragm can cover part of a vessel; and slow filling or poor mixing of contrast can make a normal vessel look pinched. This is teaching material, not a diagnosis. In this pack each narrowing is marked by a box that the dataset's cardiologists drew around it, with the degree of narrowing as a category. A box says where the narrowing is, not where its edges are: it is loose, it is often larger than the narrowing, and the same lesion's box changes size from frame to frame. A mark is graded correct when it falls inside the box. The dataset states neither how many cardiologists labelled it nor how well they agreed, gives no pixel size and no projection angle, so nothing here can be measured in millimetres.

tasks.explanation: The answer comes from the dataset's own labels for this frame. It is a statement about this one projection: an artery can look normal in one view and narrowed in another, which is why several views are taken, and the dataset only boxes what its cardiologists saw. A coronary stenosis is a narrowing of the lumen of an artery, most often from atherosclerotic plaque in the wall. An invasive angiogram shows only the lumen, filled with contrast, so a stenosis appears where the dark column of contrast becomes narrower than the normal vessel next to it: a short pinch, a long tapering, or an irregular edge. Its degree is the percentage loss of diameter against that normal reference; a narrowing of 70% or more is generally treated as obstructive and one of 50 to 69% as intermediate, where the picture alone predicts poorly whether blood flow is limited. Whether a narrowing limits flow also depends on its length, its place and the territory it supplies, which a single frame cannot tell you. A 99% narrowing leaves a hair-thin channel; in a total occlusion the vessel stops and may be filled further on from other arteries. Pitfalls: a vessel seen end-on or overlapped by another vessel hides or imitates a narrowing, so every artery is looked at in several projections; the catheter tip, the spine and the diaphragm can cover part of a vessel; and slow filling or poor mixing of contrast can make a normal vessel look pinched. This is teaching material, not a diagnosis.

tasks.explanation: The answer comes from the dataset's own labels for this frame. It is a statement about this one projection: an artery can look normal in one view and narrowed in another, which is why several views are taken, and the dataset only boxes what its cardiologists saw. A coronary stenosis is a narrowing of the lumen of an artery, most often from atherosclerotic plaque in the wall. An invasive angiogram shows only the lumen, filled with contrast, so a stenosis appears where the dark column of contrast becomes narrower than the normal vessel next to it: a short pinch, a long tapering, or an irregular edge. Its degree is the percentage loss of diameter against that normal reference; a narrowing of 70% or more is generally treated as obstructive and one of 50 to 69% as intermediate, where the picture alone predicts poorly whether blood flow is limited. Whether a narrowing limits flow also depends on its length, its place and the territory it supplies, which a single frame cannot tell you. A 99% narrowing leaves a hair-thin channel; in a total occlusion the vessel stops and may be filled further on from other arteries. Pitfalls: a vessel seen end-on or overlapped by another vessel hides or imitates a narrowing, so every artery is looked at in several projections; the catheter tip, the spine and the diaphragm can cover part of a vessel; and slow filling or poor mixing of contrast can make a normal vessel look pinched. This is teaching material, not a diagnosis.

tasks.explanation: A coronary stenosis is a narrowing of the lumen of an artery, most often from atherosclerotic plaque in the wall. An invasive angiogram shows only the lumen, filled with contrast, so a stenosis appears where the dark column of contrast becomes narrower than the normal vessel next to it: a short pinch, a long tapering, or an irregular edge. Its degree is the percentage loss of diameter against that normal reference; a narrowing of 70% or more is generally treated as obstructive and one of 50 to 69% as intermediate, where the picture alone predicts poorly whether blood flow is limited. Whether a narrowing limits flow also depends on its length, its place and the territory it supplies, which a single frame cannot tell you. A 99% narrowing leaves a hair-thin channel; in a total occlusion the vessel stops and may be filled further on from other arteries. Pitfalls: a vessel seen end-on or overlapped by another vessel hides or imitates a narrowing, so every artery is looked at in several projections; the catheter tip, the spine and the diaphragm can cover part of a vessel; and slow filling or poor mixing of contrast can make a normal vessel look pinched. This is teaching material, not a diagnosis. On this frame the box is the cardiologists' marking of the narrowing. In this pack each narrowing is marked by a box that the dataset's cardiologists drew around it, with the degree of narrowing as a category. A box says where the narrowing is, not where its edges are: it is loose, it is often larger than the narrowing, and the same lesion's box changes size from frame to frame. A mark is graded correct when it falls inside the box. The dataset states neither how many cardiologists labelled it nor how well they agreed, gives no pixel size and no projection angle, so nothing here can be measured in millimetres.

tasks.explanation: A coronary stenosis is a narrowing of the lumen of an artery, most often from atherosclerotic plaque in the wall. An invasive angiogram shows only the lumen, filled with contrast, so a stenosis appears where the dark column of contrast becomes narrower than the normal vessel next to it: a short pinch, a long tapering, or an irregular edge. Its degree is the percentage loss of diameter against that normal reference; a narrowing of 70% or more is generally treated as obstructive and one of 50 to 69% as intermediate, where the picture alone predicts poorly whether blood flow is limited. Whether a narrowing limits flow also depends on its length, its place and the territory it supplies, which a single frame cannot tell you. A 99% narrowing leaves a hair-thin channel; in a total occlusion the vessel stops and may be filled further on from other arteries. Pitfalls: a vessel seen end-on or overlapped by another vessel hides or imitates a narrowing, so every artery is looked at in several projections; the catheter tip, the spine and the diaphragm can cover part of a vessel; and slow filling or poor mixing of contrast can make a normal vessel look pinched. This is teaching material, not a diagnosis. On this frame the boxes are the cardiologists' marking of the narrowings. In this pack each narrowing is marked by a box that the dataset's cardiologists drew around it, with the degree of narrowing as a category. A box says where the narrowing is, not where its edges are: it is loose, it is often larger than the narrowing, and the same lesion's box changes size from frame to frame. A mark is graded correct when it falls inside the box. The dataset states neither how many cardiologists labelled it nor how well they agreed, gives no pixel size and no projection angle, so nothing here can be measured in millimetres.

tasks.explanation: A coronary stenosis is a narrowing of the lumen of an artery, most often from atherosclerotic plaque in the wall. An invasive angiogram shows only the lumen, filled with contrast, so a stenosis appears where the dark column of contrast becomes narrower than the normal vessel next to it: a short pinch, a long tapering, or an irregular edge. Its degree is the percentage loss of diameter against that normal reference; a narrowing of 70% or more is generally treated as obstructive and one of 50 to 69% as intermediate, where the picture alone predicts poorly whether blood flow is limited. Whether a narrowing limits flow also depends on its length, its place and the territory it supplies, which a single frame cannot tell you. A 99% narrowing leaves a hair-thin channel; in a total occlusion the vessel stops and may be filled further on from other arteries. Pitfalls: a vessel seen end-on or overlapped by another vessel hides or imitates a narrowing, so every artery is looked at in several projections; the catheter tip, the spine and the diaphragm can cover part of a vessel; and slow filling or poor mixing of contrast can make a normal vessel look pinched. This is teaching material, not a diagnosis. On this frame the box is the cardiologists' marking of the narrowing. In this pack each narrowing is marked by a box that the dataset's cardiologists drew around it, with the degree of narrowing as a category. A box says where the narrowing is, not where its edges are: it is loose, it is often larger than the narrowing, and the same lesion's box changes size from frame to frame. A mark is graded correct when it falls inside the box. The dataset states neither how many cardiologists labelled it nor how well they agreed, gives no pixel size and no projection angle, so nothing here can be measured in millimetres.

tasks.explanation: Two arteries arise from the aortic root. The right coronary artery is usually a single long vessel that runs down the right side of the heart and curves under it to the back wall. The left main artery is a short trunk that divides into the left anterior descending artery (down the front of the heart towards the apex, with diagonal branches) and the left circumflex artery (round the left side, with obtuse marginal branches); sometimes a third, intermediate branch arises between them.
